source.title: Kinetics: Rethinking Test-Time Scaling Laws
source.authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan; Zhuo Chen; Hai-Zhong Zheng; Yang Zhou; Emma Strubell; Bei-Di Chen

page_placements.theme: Inference-optimal allocation depends on task and cost accounting

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream problem-solving accuracy across model sizes and inference-time compute allocations. This is a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling, but bears on V6.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, training tokens, training compute, or compute-optimal pretraining allocations. Its results concern inference-time compute, generated tokens, and task accuracy. Sparse-attention gains are not included as rows because they compare an attention method with dense attention, rather than testing downstream predictability from scale.
record.test_reason: The study's question is inference-time compute allocation: which already-trained model size plus how many generated tokens or trials maximises reasoning accuracy under a memory-aware inference-cost budget. It trains no models. It measures no pretraining loss. It does not test whether downstream accuracy improves predictably with pretraining scale or loss. The cited Kaplan and Hoffmann laws appear only as related work and as an analogy. The Pareto-frontier results concern test-time scaling, a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version rather than V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors add that compute should go first to model size up to a critical threshold: about 14B for Qwen3, 7B for DeepSeek-distilled. They say attention cost, not parameter count, dominates test-time cost. They also claim test-time accuracy, unlike pretraining, has not saturated with compute.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates inference-time reasoning accuracy and cost across pretrained model sizes; it does not run the original pretraining-loss scaling experiments or fit their loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative Pareto performance changes with the inference strategy, model family, and cost model. The DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen series has a different dominant size from Qwen3; the max-cost versus additive-cost comparison also changes the 4B/14B Long-CoT relationship somewhat.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a memory-access-aware cost (eFLOPs), test-time compute is better spent on larger models up to about 14B (Qwen3) or 7B (DeepSeek-distilled) before adding Long-CoT length or Best-of-N trials. FLOPs-only accounting overestimates small models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time compute-optimal allocation between model size and generated tokens depends on whether memory access (KV cache) is counted in inference cost.

fits_no_version.finding: For Qwen3-8B Best-of-N with sparse attention, the optimal KV budget and generated tokens follow fitted power laws in inference cost: each cost doubling gives 1.18x KV budget and 1.74x tokens on AIME24, with similar factors on AIME25 and LiveCodeBench.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time resource allocation (KV budget versus generated tokens) scales as a power of inference compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle top-k and block top-k sparse attention raise accuracy at a fixed inference cost by up to 60 points (low cost) and about 5 points (high cost) over dense attention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse attention shifts test-time scaling frontiers.

record.problems: The study evaluates two model series, primarily from an inference perspective, and does not explore how training or post-training strategies affect the reported gaps. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the relevant results. The authors also note that their cost analysis assumes cloud serving with large batches and may not extend to local deployment.
record.rows_left_out: Sparse-attention-versus-dense results and throughput measurements were not extracted: they evaluate attention methods and efficiency rather than the scale-to-downstream-predictability relation in V6. Additional plotted results without textual numerical outcomes were also not transcribed.

untested.parts: Whether downstream accuracy improves predictably with pretraining parameters, tokens, compute or pretraining loss. No fit or prediction across pretraining scale is made.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 link is a construct mismatch. Model-size comparisons here are among fixed pretrained checkpoints under inference-cost budgets, which says nothing about predictable downstream gains from pretraining scale. The incidental note that Qwen3-32B beats 14B by only 3% on AIME24 is not a scaling test. The reader's limits_scope label on V6 should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether loss laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal pretraining parameter and training-token counts as a function of training compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices on held-out pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study measures task accuracy across model sizes and inference-time budgets, but does not test whether held-out pretraining loss predicts downstream results or fit a general predictive relationship.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or pretraining compute-optimal splits on fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen3 series
rows.operation_detail: Compared AIME24 Pass@1 across model sizes and Long-CoT generation lengths under inference-cost budgets.
rows.value: The 14B model outperforms the 4B and 8B models even at low accuracy levels (below 40%); the 0.6B model lies on the Pareto frontier only where accuracy is negligible.
rows.note: Series-level comparison reported by the authors; this is task accuracy, not a fitted power law.
rows.check: Measures which model size sits on an eFLOPs-cost Pareto frontier for AIME24 Long-CoT accuracy. That is cost-efficiency of test-time allocation, not whether accuracy improves predictably with pretraining scale or loss.

rows.subject: Qwen3 series
rows.operation_detail: Compared AIME24 solving rate across model sizes and counts of reasoning trials.
rows.value: For models smaller than 14B, increasing compute is best allocated to model scaling rather than more trials; at or above 14B, additional trials are more effective up to diminishing returns.
rows.note: The reported trend depends on model-size and trial-count regime.
rows.check: Best-of-N trial-versus-model-size allocation under an inference budget. This is a test-time scaling construct, not V6.

rows.subject: Qwen3 series
rows.size_stated: 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B, and 32B; the 0.6B model is excluded for LiveCodeBench
rows.operation_detail: Compared task performance across model sizes on additional benchmarks.
rows.measure: Task accuracy / solving rate and Pareto frontier
rows.value: Across both benchmarks, the 0.6B and 1.7B models are consistently less effective, and the Pareto frontier is almost always dominated by the 14B models.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the two benchmarks and the reported model series.
rows.check: Same Pareto-frontier dominance construct on AIME25 and LiveCodeBench. It has no bearing on predictability of downstream performance from pretraining scale.

source_check.correct: Appendix B.1 explicitly excludes the 0.6B model from LiveCodeBench evaluation. Its subsequent statement about 0.6B being less effective across both benchmarks needs that qualification; the 14B frontier-dominance statement is reported.
source_check.problem: The aggregate condition overlooks the explicit exclusion of 0.6B from LiveCodeBench, despite reproducing the authors' own inconsistent summary.

rows.subject: DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen series
rows.operation_detail: Compared AIME24 performance across model sizes and inference-time generation or trial budgets.
rows.measure: Task accuracy / solving rate and Pareto frontier
rows.value: The 1.5B model is less effective than scaling up to 7B or larger; the 7B model spans most of the Pareto frontier, and 7B Long-CoTs are reported as more efficient and effective than 14B models with short generations.
rows.note: The authors report a different dominant model size from the Qwen3 series.
rows.check: DeepSeek-distilled series frontier, where 7B dominates. The authors attribute this to KV-memory architecture, not to a scale-predictability test.

rows.subject: Qwen3 series
rows.size_stated: 4B and 14B; other series sizes also plotted
rows.operation_detail: Re-evaluated the AIME24 Long-CoT Pareto frontier using a max-cost model instead of the additive-cost model.
rows.baseline: Under the additive-cost model, the 4B and 14B models alternate until accuracy exceeds 0.4.
rows.value: Under the max-cost model, the 14B model consistently outperforms the 4B model, with a noticeable gap around accuracy 0.3 and dominance thereafter.
rows.locator: Appendix A.1, Figure 12 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors describe the overall trends as very close across cost models, with this difference in the Long-CoT comparison.
rows.check: Compares cost models (max versus additive) for the frontier. This is a cost-accounting sensitivity check, not a result on any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.correct: Appendix B.1 explicitly excludes the 0.6B model from LiveCodeBench evaluation. Its subsequent statement about 0.6B being less effective across both benchmarks needs that qualification; the 14B frontier-dominance statement is reported.
rows.problem: The aggregate condition overlooks the explicit exclusion of 0.6B from LiveCodeBench, despite reproducing the authors' own inconsistent summary.

relation.reason: It discusses pretraining scaling laws as context and contrasts them with inference-time resource allocation, without testing the listed claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates inference-cost allocation among already-trained reasoning models. It neither tests nor uses the catalog's pretraining power-law, extrapolation, training-allocation, or downstream-predictability findings.

source_check.notes: The allocation thresholds concern dense models under the study's memory-aware cloud-serving assumptions; the authors explicitly qualify applicability to local deployment. Best-of-N measures oracle coverage, and the pack abbreviates several row values.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen series on the reported reasoning benchmarks and inference budgets
reader_labels.reason: Task performance varies with model family, model-size range, and inference strategy; the reported comparisons do not establish a general predictive law from scale or pretraining loss (r1–r5).
